identified_problem: Unsupervised formats are rated Weak on capability verification, GenAI exposure and authorship assurance. GenAI can complete most standard take-home programming tasks [R28], [R84], [R90], [D03], and take-home marks overstated individual capability compared with vivas and proctored exams [R81], [R96], [D24]. Similarity tools, detectors and markers could not reliably identify AI-produced work, and marking did not respond to the share of AI-authored code [R08], [S009], [R52], [J1].
recommended_redesign: Keep unsupervised work as the scalable main assessment, but pair it with a short individual check of understanding, such as a viva or live demonstration on the student's own artefact [R81], [R80], [J4].
Mark critique, verification and design reasoning, for example critique of AI output and justification of accepted or rejected suggestions, rather than only the final output [R09], [R91], [R44].
Pre-test each task against current GenAI tools and recheck it every teaching cycle, because AI-resistant constraints are expected to erode [R82], [R83], [S030].
Keep unsupervised online quizzes for low-stakes formative use, permit only AI tools all students can access, and structure and limit any AI-log submissions [S001], [R12], [R15], [R20], [S123], [R17].
justification: Finding: in a 60-student programming module, adding a repository with version history, a structured viva and a supervised live demo raised a learning-integrity score from about 11.7 to about 45.3, and 86.7% of students rated the redesign fair [R81]; 10-minute individual vivas on a GenAI-permitted project ran with over 750 students and separated members of the same group [R80]. Finding: a summative task that had students critique ChatGPT output and reflect on their prompting was run in a computing module [R09]. Interpretation: the unsupervised artefact on its own says little about individual understanding, so its value depends on marking reasoning and critique and on adding a separate individual check [R81], [R84].
implementation_considerations: Cohort: the format itself scales, with reported use for 120-150 students with automated grading and over 750 students across two campuses [R25], [R80]; the added check is what drives cost, at about 1,000 staff minutes per 100 students for 10-minute interviews [R84].
Staff time: rubric marking replaces autograding for open-ended projects, long AI-conversation submissions made marking slower, and AI-resilient items need extra question writing [R82], [S123], [R25].
Equity: paid tools outperformed free ones, so permit only tools all students can access or provide them; detector-based judgements can disadvantage non-native writers [S001], [R20], [R15], [R28].

Policy: declarations and AI logs improve transparency but were often poor, unusable or fabricated, and logged AI-use behaviour did not identify which students had larger assignment-exam gaps, so they should not be treated as proof of understanding [R45], [R17], [R72], [J6], [D26].
Tools: only 5.3% of capstone students used a university-hosted GenAI instance, so a university tool cannot be assumed to be the one students use [D14].
evidence_status_basis: Similar redesigns were implemented in computing courses (computing = Y in tested_redesigns.md): take-home work paired with a structured viva and supervised live demo, with descriptive before and after scores for 60 students [R81]; a GenAI-permitted group project with submitted prompts and 10-minute individual vivas for over 750 students, reported descriptively [R80]; a summative task requiring critique of ChatGPT output and reflection on prompting, with 17 learners [R09]; and required, declared GenAI use with marks for prompts and verification in a foundation-year module of 88 students [R15]. None had a control group, so outcomes are descriptive.
risks_and_limits: The redesign cannot make the unsupervised artefact itself secure: GenAI can still produce critiques, reflections and justifications, and some students completed GenAI requirements performatively [R91], [R45]. The individual check verifies understanding at one point but does not show who produced each part [R81]. AI-resistant constraints are likely to erode as models improve, and most capability benchmarks use 2023-2024 models [R83], [S030], [D03]. No controlled computing study compares redesigned and conventional unsupervised tasks.
